judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass HB 1222, the Maryland Values Act, which limited federal immigration enforcement at "sensitive locations" in Maryland. A federal law enforcement officer must notify specified individuals about an immigration enforcement action at such a location. A public school, a public library, or a state or local executive agency operating a sensitive location must deny immigration agents access to any portion not open to the general public, unless the agent presents a valid judicial warrant or exigent circumstances exist. That access rule does not reach correctional facilities or courthouse detention facilities. The Attorney General must publish guidance, each covered entity had to adopt a matching policy by October 1, 2025, and by July 1, 2026 each must publish procedures preventing the sale or redisclosure of personal records and geolocation data in ways that harm residents' privacy. The Maryland House of Delegates passed it 101-38 and it was signed into law as Chapter 718 of 2025.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass HB 1424, the Protect Our Federal Workers Act, which opened state assistance to Marylanders who lost federal jobs. This emergency bill widened the purposes of the Catastrophic Event Account and renamed the shutdown loan fund the Federal Government Employee Assistance Loan Fund, so both may help former federal employees. It changed who may borrow from that fund, allowed loan forgiveness, and authorized moving $5.0 million from the Rainy Day Fund into it in fiscal 2025. It expanded the Attorney General's powers under the Maryland Defense Act and raised that office's mandated appropriation to at least $2.5 million. It also set up a temporary Expedited Hiring Program to place people who left federal service into vacant skilled and professional state jobs. The Maryland House of Delegates passed it 105-33 and it was signed into law as Chapter 97 of 2025.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass HB 424, the Lowering Prescription Drug Costs for All Marylanders Now Act, which expanded what the Prescription Drug Affordability Board may do about high drug prices. It repealed the board's upper payment limit reporting requirements. In their place the board must decide whether setting upper payment limits is in the state's best interest for drugs that have caused or will cause an affordability challenge, and must set them if it so decides. The board may set those limits by regulation for drugs bought or paid for by state and local government units. The board may not enforce a limit against Medicare Part C or D reimbursement rules, count a pharmacy dispensing fee toward a limit, or apply a new limit to a drug in a current shortage. The bill added members to the stakeholder council, and its requirement that the board set limits on all purchases and payor reimbursements is contingent on specified actions taking place by September 30, 2030. The Maryland House of Delegates passed it 100-38 and it was signed into law as Chapter 611 of 2025.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass SB 901, which made producers of packaging and paper products responsible for recycling what they sell. Each producer must submit a producer responsibility plan to the Maryland Department of the Environment for review and approval by July 1, 2028. Beginning on a date the department sets, a producer may not sell, distribute, or import covered materials for sale in Maryland without an approved plan. The department must build a statewide list of covered materials, run an ongoing statewide recycling needs assessment, and enforce the framework. The bill also changed the existing Producer Responsibility Advisory Council and set rules for service providers. The Maryland Senate passed it 33-11 and it was signed into law as Chapter 431 of 2025.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass HB 767, which added notice requirements and tenant remedies late in an eviction. Once a court issues a warrant of restitution in a failure to pay rent, breach of lease, or tenant holding over case, the landlord must give the tenant written notice at least six days before the repossession date the sheriff has set. The bill gave tenants civil remedies against a landlord who breaks those rules. It applies only going forward, and does not reach any cause of action filed before its effective date. The Maryland House of Delegates passed it 97-41 and it was signed into law as Chapter 563 of 2025.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass SB 848, which created the Public Health Abortion Grant Program to improve access to abortion care clinical services. The money comes from surplus sitting in insurance carriers' segregated abortion-care accounts under the federal Affordable Care Act. The Insurance Commissioner must order those funds transferred into a new state fund, and the Governor had to allocate $2.0 million of them to the program by October 1, 2025. Starting in fiscal 2027 the Governor must budget at least 90% of the qualifying account surplus for the fund each year. The Maryland Senate passed it 29-15 and it was signed into law as Chapter 436 of 2025.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass HB 1378, which cut what child sexual abuse victims can recover in claims that had been time-barred until Maryland reopened them. It lowered the liability limits for those claims under the Maryland Tort Claims Act, the Local Government Tort Claims Act, and the provisions covering local boards of education. It lowered the cap on noneconomic damages in other previously time-barred child sexual abuse actions. It also switched those limits from applying per incident or occurrence to applying per claim, and capped the counsel fees a victim's lawyer may charge in these cases. The Maryland House of Delegates passed it 91-41 and it was signed into law as Chapter 104 of 2025.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass HB 39, the Carlton R. Smith Act, which repealed Maryland's HIV transfer crime. The bill struck the misdemeanor prohibition on knowingly transferring or attempting to transfer HIV to another person, along with its penalty. The Maryland House of Delegates passed it 100-36 and it was signed into law as Chapter 651 of 2025.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass HB 983, which created a Language Assistance Program for voters who need a language other than English. The State Board of Elections must identify, on stated criteria, the counties with a significant need for such assistance. Local boards in those counties must provide the listed services, including an option for a voter to reach a translator in order to communicate with election judges at an early voting center or a polling place. The state board had to publish and maintain the list of covered local boards on its website by January 1, 2026. The Maryland House of Delegates passed it 97-30 and it was signed into law as Chapter 278 of 2025.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass HB 1020, the Fair Medical Debt Reporting Act, which kept medical debt out of consumer credit reports. A consumer reporting agency may not include specified medical debt information in a consumer report, and no one may use such information to judge creditworthiness. A business whose primary work is providing medical services, products, or devices may not report any part of a medical debt to a consumer reporting agency. Such a business must also write that prohibition into any contract selling or assigning medical debt for collection, and a contract signed after the effective date without that term is void and unenforceable. The Maryland House of Delegates passed it 102-37 and it was signed into law as Chapter 121 of 2025.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass HB 197, which told the state to plan for restorative practices schools. By July 1, 2026 the Maryland State Department of Education must develop a comprehensive plan for establishing such schools, drawing on subject matter experts, and must provide technical assistance on request. A local board of education that chooses to establish one must use that plan. The department must report on the plan to the Governor and the General Assembly by December 1, 2026, and the state's school discipline guidelines now name restorative practices rather than approaches. The Maryland House of Delegates passed it 94-36 and it was signed into law as Chapter 240 of 2025.
